A reader can tell exactly what was run.
- **The paper is candid about what complicates its story, in places.** The Table 2 note (p. 10) and the Discussion (p. 22) say plainly that 69 of 74 TWDL hot spots are in El Paso County and that there is "no consistent statewide association" outside it. The Austin and Houston tract sections (pp. 16–18) say the local pattern "complicates the county-level marketization narrative." Hedges on cold spots ("potentially reflecting campus size, capacity constraints, or implementation stage," p. 14) and on scope ("cannot follow an individual family," p. 23) are good practice.
- **The tract-level maps (Figures 10–15, pp. 18–21) are the paper's most legible exhibits.** They distinguish program type by marker shape, have full legends and scale bars, and show recognizable place names. The prose in those sections tracks them reasonably well, apart from the exceptions noted below.
- **Disclosure of AI assistance in data preparation is specific** (p. 6; Acknowledgements, p. 24).

**Weaknesses:**

- **The headline contradicts the paper's own table (checkable).** The abstract (p. 1) says "TWDL programs cluster in more affluent, lower-immigrant areas," and the Discussion (p. 21) says "it is mostly affluent areas with low immigrant density that have access to TWDL." The Table 2 note (p. 10) says there is "no consistent statewide association between TWDL hot spot status and either immigrant density or income outside this single county." Table 2's own cells put TWDL hot spots mostly in *lower*-income and *higher*-immigrant bins (details in check 6). The abstract never mentions the El Paso concentration or the tract-level co-location finding, which are the two results that most change how the headline should be read.
- **Specific Findings sentences are contradicted by Table 2 (checkable).** Three examples: p. 11 says counties at or above \$70,000 "represented the majority of [TWDL] hot spot locations," but Table 2 gives 13 of 73 (18%). p. 9 says the 36%+ foreign-born counties "had the fewest TWDL hot spots," but Table 2 gives 7, which ties the 6–10% bin and exceeds the 0–5% bin (3). p. 11 says the \$91K+ counties "show almost no OWDL hot spots," but Table 2 gives 73 (47.4%).
- **Table 2 does not reconcile with itself (checkable).** The immigrant-density panel sums to 720 TWDL and 1,091 OWDL campuses, which matches the stated exclusions. The income panel sums to 716 and 1,089 with no explanation, and its hot-spot totals (73 and 585) differ from the density panel (74 and 587). The note's "69 of 74 statewide hot spots" in El Paso County cannot be squared with county-level bins in which no TWDL bin holds more than 40 hot spots in either panel.
- **Other count discrepancies with no stated reconciliation (checkable).** Table 1 (p. 5) lists 1,226 TWDL and 1,351 OWDL campuses, but the analysis uses 729 and 1,097 (p. 7). That drops 41% of TWDL campuses and 19% of OWDL campuses, and the only explanation is "charter and alternative campuses were excluded." Table 1's Early Exit count is also exactly 1,226, identical to TWDL. The "8,115 bilingual programs" figure (p. 5) does not match any sum of Table 1's rows.
- **Several readings of the maps don't match the maps (checkable by viewing).** Examples: TWDL cold spots are said to be "widespread across the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, Houston, and Austin" (p. 14), but Figure 3 shows those metros mostly not significant, and Table 2 counts only 40 TWDL cold spots statewide. The text describes "a small cluster [of TWDL hot spots] near San Antonio" (p. 13), but Figures 3 and 9 show no hot-spot marker near San Antonio. The Rio Grande Valley is described as an area where TWDL was "largely absent or present only as cold spots" (p. 10), but Figures 3 and 9 show TWDL campuses there classified as not significant.
- **Contradictions between sections on the El Paso mechanism.** p. 9 attributes the El Paso TWDL hot spot to "employment at the university." The tract-level Findings (p. 21) place TWDL *cold* spots "in proximity to the University of Texas at El Paso." The Discussion (p. 22) then says "TWDL programs are nearest to the university."
- **Some constructs in the abstract and question have no exhibit behind them.** "Urbanicity" appears in the abstract, the research question, and the Discussion, but it is never measured or mapped as a variable. Statements about "white, affluent families" (pp. 22, 24) are not tied to any racial-composition data in the exhibits. That is legitimate theoretical interpretation, but a reader should not take it as a finding.
- **The paper's vocabulary for hot and cold spots invites misreading.** "Hot spot" is glossed as "campuses with high enrollment ratios" (pp. 9–10). At other points it is used as if it meant program presence or "access" (e.g., "Counties with lower immigrant density and higher wealth had access to TWDL programs," p. 9). With a 170 km fixed band, a hot or cold classification describes a region, not a single campus, and it is conditional on the program already existing there. "Not significant" is also read as "inconsistent enrollment" or "spatial isolation" (pp. 17–18). Readers should be careful with both.
- **Figure design limits self-containment.** In Figures 3–8, the "Cold Spot with 90% Confidence" color is a light gray that is hard to tell apart from "Not Significant." County choropleths carry no county labels, so a reader cannot identify which bin El Paso or the Rio Grande Valley counties fall into. In Figure 9, TWDL squares are drawn over OWDL circles, which hides the OWDL cold-spot clusters around Austin–San Antonio and Houston that are obvious in Figure 6. No figure marks the universities that the text relies on as an explanation.
- **Referencing lapses (checkable).** "(“Hot Spot Analysis,” 2023)" on p. 8 has no matching reference entry. The Methods specify ACS **5-year** estimates (p. 6), but the reference URLs for both tables point to **1-year** products (`ACSST1Y2021.S1903`, `ACSDT1Y2021.B05012`; p. 26). There is a stray "(Bell, 1992, )" on p. 3, and Bell (1995) appears in the references without a text citation.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Read Table 2 (p. 10) and its note before anything else in the Findings.** The cell counts are the only quantitative summary of the hot-spot results. The note's El Paso caveat is the single most important qualifier in the paper. Before quoting any statement of the form "TWDL hot spots are in affluent / low-immigrant counties," check it against the TWDL rows. They generally do not support it.
- **Do not quote the abstract's TWDL sentence, the p. 9 TWDL paragraphs, the p. 11 "\$70,000 or greater" sentence, the p. 21 Discussion opener, or the Conclusion's "TWDL will continue to follow the geography of white, affluent growth" as empirical findings.** The paper's own more careful statement is on p. 22: TWDL hot spots are concentrated in one county, and outside it there is no consistent association.
- **The OWDL density pattern is the better-supported comparative finding.** OWDL hot-spot shares rise from roughly 44–47% in the 0–20% foreign-born bins to 58–63% in the 21%+ bins (Table 2). Even so, the p. 11 claim of "almost no" OWDL hot spots in the highest-income counties is wrong by the table: 73 hot spots, or 47.4%.
- **Treat "hot spot" and "cold spot" as regional classifications of enrollment share among campuses that already offer the program.** With a 170 km band (p. 8), whole metros share a label: all DFW OWDL campuses are hot, and most Austin–San Antonio OWDL campuses are cold (Figure 6). The classification does not tell you who is enrolled, whether ML students are served, or where programs are absent.
- **The tract-level sections (pp. 15–21, Figures 10–15) are worth reading, not skimming.** The paper says they "complicate" the county story in Austin and Houston: TWDL and OWDL hot spots co-locate in moderate-income, immigrant-dense corridors. The abstract omits this entirely.
- **Can skim:** the literature review and theoretical framework (pp. 2–4) if you know the TWDL-gentrification literature, and the general descriptions of GIS, the Census, and TIGER/Line (pp. 4–5).
- **Check sample sizes yourself.** Use 720 TWDL and 1,091 OWDL campuses for the density panel and 716 and 1,089 for the income panel, not 729 and 1,097. Remember that about 40% of Table 1's TWDL campuses are not in the analysis. The online appendices and ICPSR deposit were not available for this review, so I could not check whether they resolve these discrepancies.

**Detailed Commentary:**

#### Organization and navigability
The macro-structure is conventional and works. There is a short introduction, a history/gentrification literature review, a CRT/raciolinguistic framework that ends in an explicit research question (p. 4), a methods section that walks through the pipeline, and a Findings section organized around 15 figures and one table. The research question is restated at the start of Findings (p. 9), which helps.

Navigation breaks down inside the Findings. The load-bearing quantitative exhibit, Table 2, is introduced on p. 9 as "a quantitative complement" to Figures 3–9, but the TWDL narrative that immediately follows (p. 9) never cites a single Table 2 number. It makes claims the table contradicts. The El Paso qualifier, which changes the interpretation of the whole TWDL analysis, lives in the table note (p. 10) and resurfaces only in one Discussion paragraph (p. 22). The abstract, the county-level Findings text, the opening of the Discussion (p. 21), and the Conclusion (p. 24) all carry the original "TWDL in affluent, low-immigrant areas" account. The result is two incompatible accounts of the TWDL pattern side by side, and a reader who stops at the abstract or at the p. 9 Findings gets the one the table does not support.

#### Fidelity of argument
The rhetoric outruns the results most clearly on TWDL. Table 2 shows that 606 of 720 TWDL campuses (84%) are not significant. Hot spots are 74 (10%) and cold spots are 40 (6%) (p. 10, Table 2, density panel; my sums). By the note's own account, hot spots are overwhelmingly one county's campuses. Hot-spot rates are highest in the 21–35% foreign-born bin (16.1%) and the \$0–40K income bin (18.7%). Those are the opposite of "affluent, lower-immigrant." Cold spots are few, and none are in the 36%+ bin. On that evidence, the p. 9 conclusion that hot spots sit "in counties with low immigrant population and higher median household incomes and cold spots within counties with high immigrant population and lower median household incomes" is not supported.

The paper then builds its theoretical reading of "extraction" and "mining" (pp. 21–22) on that unsupported pattern. On the paper's own terms, the CRSA reading would need to rest on the OWDL density gradient and the tract-level evidence, not on the county TWDL hot-spot geography.

Two interpretive moves also go beyond what Gi* delivers, and readers should discount them:

1. El Paso is a TWDL hot spot and an OWDL cold spot, and p. 12 reads this as meaning "TWDL campuses there have higher proportional enrollment relative to OWDL campuses." Each Gi* run compares a program's ratios with that same program's statewide distribution, so the two labels do not establish a TWDL-versus-OWDL comparison within El Paso. This is an interpretive judgment.
2. "Not significant" is repeatedly read as "internal inconsistency," "spatial isolation," or "inconsistent enrollment" (pp. 17–18, 21). A non-significant Gi* z-score is also what homogeneous moderate values produce. This is an interpretive judgment.

The ANNA paragraph (p. 9) concludes that "program-specific spatial forces are shaping program placement." The evidence is that ratios of 0.190 and 0.207 are lower than 0.317 for all campuses. No test of that difference is reported, and ANN ratios for subsets of different sizes drawn from an already clustered population are not directly comparable. This is interpretive, but the causal language ("forces are shaping") is stronger than a descriptive comparison supports.

#### Abstract fidelity
The abstract describes the method (CRSA, placement relative to immigrant density, urbanicity, and socioeconomics) and the OWDL finding in a way the paper broadly supports. It overstates the TWDL finding (see check 6). It lists "urbanicity," which is never operationalized. It omits (a) the El Paso concentration of TWDL hot spots, (b) the paper's own statement that there is no consistent statewide TWDL association, (c) the tract-level co-location of TWDL and OWDL in Austin and Houston, and (d) that the analysis is a single-year (2020–21), campus-level, cross-sectional description. A reader relying on the abstract would come away with a stronger and simpler conclusion than the body supports.

#### Tables and figures

- **Table 2 (p. 10)** is the paper's most important exhibit and is clearly laid out: bins, program, n (%), totals. The percentages are internally correct: I recomputed every cell, and all row percentages match their row totals. However, the panel totals disagree (check 1), and the note's El Paso statement cannot be squared with county-level bins (check 2). It also reports only binned marginals, so claims about joint "higher income *and* lower immigrant density" (p. 22) cannot be checked against it.
- **Figures 3–9 (pp. 11–17)** carry the county-level argument. Base map, legend, north arrow, and scale are present. However, the 90% cold-spot and not-significant symbols are nearly the same gray, counties are unlabeled, and Figure 9's overplotting hides OWDL cold spots. Figures 3 and 6 have no demographic layer, so the reader must flip between 3/4/5 and 6/7/8 to relate points to bins. A reader cannot confirm from these maps which bin El Paso County falls into. In my visual reading, El Paso County is shaded a mid-purple in Figure 4 (p. 12) and a light green in Figure 5 (p. 13). The darkest 36%+ shade appears on only a few sparsely populated far-west counties adjacent to El Paso. That makes Table 2's 70 TWDL and 158 OWDL campuses in the 36%+ bin hard to reconcile visually. This is a judgment from reading the map, not a checkable fact.
- **Figures 10–15 (pp. 18–21)** are better: distinct shapes for the two programs, named places, legible legends. The tract choropleth shading is faint enough that distinguishing adjacent classes is difficult, especially in Figures 10 and 12.

#### Density and length
The paper runs 27 pages with 15 figures. The county-level Findings repeat the same legend-reading boilerplate twice (pp. 9 and 10). The literature review and methods-context sections are longer than the analytic payload needs. The essential material comes to about six pages: pp. 7–10 (analysis choices and Table 2), p. 13 (Figure 9), pp. 16–21 (tract-level), and p. 22 (the El Paso paragraph).

#### Text-versus-exhibit checks

1. **Table 2 totals vs. analysis samples, and cross-panel agreement.** Claim: analysis samples are 729 TWDL and 1,097 OWDL, less 9 and 6 geometry-error exclusions (p. 7; p. 10, Table 2 note). Numbers (my sums from p. 10, Table 2):
   - Density panel: TWDL 43+104+255+248+70 = **720** (= 729 − 9); OWDL 53+114+341+425+158 = **1,091** (= 1,097 − 6). CONSISTENT.
   - Income panel: TWDL 134+173+131+125+153 = **716**; OWDL 208+293+235+199+154 = **1,089**. INCONSISTENT; 4 TWDL and 2 OWDL campuses are unaccounted for.
   - Category totals across panels: TWDL hot/cold/not significant are 74/40/606 (density) vs **73/40/603** (income); OWDL are 587/423/81 vs **585/423/81**. INCONSISTENT; no note explains the difference (e.g., missing income data).
   - Verdict: **INCONSISTENT** (income panel).

2. **"69 of 74 statewide hot spots (93%)" in El Paso County (p. 10, Table 2 note; repeated p. 22).** The note says bins are county-level ACS values, so every El Paso County campus must fall into a single density bin and a single income bin. The largest TWDL hot-spot count in any density bin is 40 (21–35%), and in any income bin it is 25 (\$0–40K) (p. 10, Table 2). Sixty-nine hot spots from one county cannot fit in any one bin. The note's corollary also fails: "excluding El Paso, fewer than 2% of TWDL campuses in any bin are hot spots." Only 5 non–El Paso hot spots would exist, yet the bins outside 21–35% alone hold 3+7+17+7 = 34 hot spots. The note is arithmetically incompatible with the table it annotates, and I cannot tell which is correct. Figure 3 (p. 11) does visually show nearly all TWDL hot-spot markers in El Paso, which supports the note's substance over the table's binning. Verdict: **INCONSISTENT**.

3. **"Counties with median incomes of \$70,000 or greater represented the majority of [TWDL] hot spot locations" (p. 11).** Table 2 income panel (p. 10): \$71–90K = 5 and \$91K+ = 8, so 13 of 73 hot spots (17.8%). The \$0–40K bin alone has 25 (34%), and 60 of 73 (82%) are below \$71K. Figure 5 (p. 13) agrees visually: the El Paso hot-spot cluster sits on a light-green (lower-income) county, and no TWDL hot-spot marker sits on a dark-green county. Verdict: **INCONSISTENT**.

4. **"The counties with the highest immigrant density (36%+ foreign-born ...) had the fewest TWDL hot spots" (p. 9).** Table 2 (p. 10): the 36%+ bin has 7 hot spots, versus 3 (0–5%), 7 (6–10%), 17 (11–20%), and 40 (21–35%). By count, it ties for second-fewest. By rate, its 10.0% is the *second-highest*, after 21–35% (16.1%). The same paragraph's claim of "cold spots within counties with high immigrant population" also conflicts with the table's **0** cold spots in the 36%+ bin. Verdict: **INCONSISTENT**.

5. **"Cold spots were more broadly distributed, covering 25 counties across the state, with 76% located in counties with higher median household income and lower immigrant density" (p. 22).** Table 2 (p. 10) has 40 TWDL cold spots. It does not report county counts, so "25 counties" cannot be checked. Taking the most generous cutoffs, the share of cold spots in the 0–20% foreign-born bins is 23/40 = 57.5%, and the share at \$56K+ is 24/40 = 60%. The joint share can be no larger than 57.5%, well below 76%. The 76% might be a share of the 25 counties (19 of 25), not of campuses, but no exhibit reports that. Under the paper's own "lower immigrant density" reference point (state county mean 9.3%, p. 7), only 6/40 = 15% of cold spots qualify. Verdict: **INCONSISTENT** as a campus share; unverifiable as a county share.

6. **Abstract (p. 1) and Discussion (p. 21): "TWDL programs cluster in more affluent, lower-immigrant areas" / "mostly affluent areas with low immigrant density ... have access to TWDL."**
   - Against the Table 2 note (p. 10): "no consistent statewide association ... outside this single county." Directly contradictory.
   - Against TWDL hot spots (p. 10, Table 2): 47 of 74 (63.5%) are in the 21%+ foreign-born bins, and 44 of 73 (60.3%) are in the ≤\$55K bins.
   - Against where TWDL campuses are (p. 10, Table 2 totals; my computations): only 147 of 720 TWDL campuses (20.4%) are in 0–10% foreign-born counties, and 278 of 716 (38.8%) are in ≥\$71K counties. Relative to OWDL there is a modest difference: TWDL has 44.2% vs OWDL 53.4% in the 21%+ bins, and 38.8% vs 32.4% in the ≥\$71K bins. That supports at most a comparative statement ("TWDL campuses are somewhat less concentrated than OWDL in high-immigrant, lower-income counties"), not "cluster in affluent, lower-immigrant areas."
   - Verdict: **INCONSISTENT**.

7. **Table 1 (p. 5) vs. analysis samples (p. 7).** Table 1 gives TWDL = 1,226 and OWDL = 1,351, and the text on p. 5 repeats both. The analysis uses 729 and 1,097 (p. 7). That drops 497 TWDL campuses (40.5%) and 254 OWDL campuses (18.8%), explained only by the exclusion of "charter and alternative campuses" (p. 7), with no count of either. Table 1 also lists Early Exit Transitional Bilingual as exactly **1,226**, identical to TWDL, which a reader should treat as a possible transcription error. The p. 5 statement that "there were 8,115 bilingual programs being implemented across schools (n = 7,134)" matches no sum of Table 1: all six rows total 13,865, and the four bilingual rows total 4,267. Verdict: **INCONSISTENT** (unreconciled attrition; suspicious duplicate; 8,115 unmatched).

8. **ANN ratios and "approximately 40% lower" (p. 9).**
   - Ratios: 0.190/0.317 = 0.599 (TWDL 40% lower); 0.207/0.317 = 0.653 (OWDL 35% lower). "Approximately 40%" is accurate for TWDL and generous for OWDL.
   - Reported distances match the ratios: 2,946/15,542 = 0.190 and 2,619/12,626 = 0.207.
   - Sample size behind the distances: the expected distance under the standard formula 0.5·√(A/n), with A = 695,662 km² (p. 7), gives 15,542 m only for n = **720** and 12,626 m only for n = **1,091**. For the stated n = 729 and 1,097 it gives 15,446 m and 12,591 m. So the ANNA appears to have been run on the post-exclusion samples, not the n reported on pp. 7 and 9.
   - The claim that clustering "exceeds what general school geography alone would predict" rests on comparing ratios, with no test (interpretive; see Fidelity above).
   - Verdict: **CONSISTENT** on the ratio arithmetic (loosely for OWDL); **INCONSISTENT** on the stated n.

9. **Citations and data references.**
   - "(“Hot Spot Analysis,” 2023)" on p. 8 has no corresponding entry in the reference list (pp. 24–27).
   - The Methods (p. 6) specify "2021 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates" and justify 5-year over 1-year data, but the reference URLs for U.S. Census Bureau 2021a/2021b (p. 26) point to `tid=ACSST1Y2021.S1903` and `tid=ACSDT1Y2021.B05012`, the **1-year** tables. S1903 is also described as a "Detailed Table" (p. 6) when it is a Subject Table.
   - The ANN formula is cited to "Esri, 2022," whose reference entry is the ArcGIS Pro software itself (p. 25).
   - Minor: stray "(Bell, 1992, )" (p. 3); Bell (1995) is listed in the references (p. 24) but not cited; the Valdez et al. (2016) entry spells "Delevan" (p. 27) while the text has "Delavan."
   - Verdict: **INCONSISTENT**.

10. **"The highest income counties (those in the \$91,000+ range) show almost no OWDL hot spots" (p. 11).** Table 2 (p. 10): \$91K+ OWDL has 73 hot spots out of 154 (47.4%), about the same rate as the other income bins (49–60%). Visually, Figure 8 (p. 16) shows the DFW OWDL hot-spot cluster covering dark-green counties. Verdict: **INCONSISTENT**.

11. **"The counties with the lowest immigrant density ... show almost no OWDL hot spots" (p. 10).** Table 2 (p. 10): 0–5% OWDL has 25 hot spots out of 53 (47.2%), and 6–10% has 50 out of 114 (43.9%). There are fewer hot spots by count, but the rate is not "almost no." Verdict: **INCONSISTENT** (overstated).

12. **"OWDL hot spots at 99% confidence sit predominantly within counties of 11%–20% and 21%–35%+" (p. 10) and "concentrated in ... \$41,000–\$55,000 and \$56,000–\$70,000" (p. 11).** Table 2 collapses confidence levels. At all levels, 153 + 267 = 420 of 587 hot spots (71.6%) are in 11–35%, and 163 + 140 = 303 of 585 (51.8%) are in \$41–70K. The direction is right; "concentrated" is a bare majority for income. Verdict: **CONSISTENT** (loosely for income).

13. **"TWDL cold spots are widespread across the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, Houston, and Austin" (p. 14).** Table 2 (p. 10) has 40 TWDL cold spots statewide (5.6% of 720). In Figure 3 (p. 11), DFW, Houston, and Austin TWDL campuses appear predominantly as not-significant gray points. The saturated blue cold-spot markers visible are near Waco, east of Austin, south-west of Houston, and at Laredo on the border. The near-identical grays for 90% cold spots and not-significant points make exact counts impossible. Verdict: **INCONSISTENT** (visual reading; "widespread" overstated).

14. **"TWDL hot spots ... El Paso in the far west, a small cluster near San Antonio, and scattered points in the north-central corridor" (p. 13).** In Figures 3 (p. 11) and 9 (p. 17), no hot-spot marker appears near San Antonio. The non–El Paso hot-spot markers are one near Corpus Christi and two 90% markers in northeast Texas. Verdict: **INCONSISTENT** (visual reading).

15. **Rio Grande Valley described as where "TWDL programs were largely absent or present only as cold spots" (p. 10).** Figures 3 (p. 11) and 9 (p. 17) show TWDL campus markers in the lower Rio Grande Valley classified as not significant (gray), not absent and not cold. Verdict: **INCONSISTENT** (visual reading).

16. **El Paso and the university explanation (pp. 9, 21, 22).** p. 9 says the El Paso TWDL hot spot is "likely connected to employment at the university." The tract-level Findings say "TWDL cold spots concentrate in the downtown and near-downtown area in proximity to the University of Texas at El Paso" (p. 21). The Discussion says "TWDL programs are nearest to the university" (p. 22). No figure marks UTEP (Figures 14–15, pp. 20–21), so the reader cannot adjudicate. Verdict: **INCONSISTENT** (text vs. text).

17. **El Paso tract-level zones (p. 18/21 vs. Figure 14, p. 20).** The text describes a "far west side" zone of TWDL hot spots "at 99% confidence." In Figure 14, the 99% (dark red) TWDL squares cluster in central El Paso along the border by Juárez. The westernmost significant TWDL markers are lighter (90–95%) squares, and the upper west side is mostly not significant, which the text also says. The text also says OWDL hot spots "extend ... toward San Elizario, Fabens, and Tornillo" and, a few lines later, that the San Elizario and Fabens OWDL campuses are not significant. Figure 14 shows gray markers at San Elizario and Fabens and orange (hot) markers only near Tornillo. The claim that El Paso is "uniformly high in immigrant density" (p. 18) sits beside large 0–10% tracts in Figure 14 (Fort Bliss and the northeast). Verdict: **AMBIGUOUS** (partly consistent; internal wording conflicts).

18. **Austin: "only a single isolated TWDL cold spot appears in [the northern suburbs]" (p. 17).** In Figure 10 (p. 18), the saturated blue markers near Round Rock are OWDL *circles* (99% and 95% cold). Three or four pale TWDL cold-spot *squares* (90%) appear in the same area. The pale legend shading makes this hard to judge. Verdict: **AMBIGUOUS**, leaning inconsistent.

19. **Houston: "Statistically significant cold spots are nearly absent ... appearing as only two isolated points south of the metro" (p. 18).** Figure 13 (p. 20) shows two OWDL cold circles in the south (near Pearland and Sugar Land) and one TWDL cold square north of the center. The count is roughly right, but one point is north, not south. Verdict: **CONSISTENT** (minor discrepancy).

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

This paper maps where two-way (TWDL) and one-way (OWDL) dual language programs sit across Texas in 2020–21, combining campus locations with county- and tract-level immigrant density and median income. That makes it the first statewide campus-level picture of the question, and the Austin and Houston tract results (TWDL and OWDL hot spots in the same places) are a useful, honestly reported complication. The abstract's headline claim does not survive the paper's own Table 2. That claim is that TWDL clusters in affluent, lower-immigrant areas and OWDL in higher-immigrant, lower-income ones. In the table, TWDL hot-spot rates are highest in the highest-immigrant and lowest-income bins, 93% of TWDL hot spots sit in a single border county, and the table note concedes "no consistent statewide association." The descriptive map is a real contribution, but the claim most likely to be cited overstates it.

**Strengths:**

- **A new statewide descriptive base.** [Checkable] The paper links TEA's 2020–21 campus-level program data, obtained through a public information request (p. 5), to ACS 5-year tract and county estimates. It then maps 729 public TWDL campuses and 1,097 public OWDL campuses (p. 7), and I am not aware of an earlier campus-level statewide map of TWDL versus OWDL placement in Texas. Most prior Texas work cited here is case-based and qualitative (Heiman & Murakami, 2019; Dorner et al., 2021; Chávez-Moreno, 2021; pp. 3, 21). A statewide picture is the natural complement to that work.
- **Both program types are compared, not TWDL alone.** Looking at OWDL next to TWDL (pp. 5, 9–13) changes the question from "is TWDL in rich places?" to "which kind of dual language reaches which communities?" That framing is sharper, and the rest of the field can reuse it.
- **A multi-scale result that runs against the paper's own story, reported honestly.** [Checkable against the maps] In Austin (Figure 10, p. 18; Figure 11, p. 19) and Houston (Figures 12–13, pp. 19–20), the locally re-run Gi* analysis puts TWDL and OWDL hot spots in the same moderate-income, immigrant-dense corridors, not in separate territories (pp. 16–18). I checked Figure 10: TWDL squares and OWDL circles cluster together along central and East Austin. The author says outright that this "complicates the county-level marketization narrative" (p. 17). In my judgment this is the paper's most credible and most original substantive finding.
- **Program intensity, not raw headcount.** Using the program enrollment ratio (program enrollment divided by campus enrollment) as the Gi* input (pp. 7–8) avoids hot spots that simply reflect large campuses.
- **Useful framing of policy levels.** The Limitations section (p. 23) separates availability (a district and state issue) from access within neighborhoods (catchment, transfer, and enrollment practice). It also names comparison with early-exit and ESL programs as possibly the bigger equity question. Both give follow-on work a sensible agenda.

**Weaknesses:**

- **The headline finding runs against the paper's own Table 2.** [Checkable, Table 2, p. 10] Share of TWDL campuses that are hot spots, by county immigrant-density bin: 7.0%, 6.7%, 6.7%, **16.1%** (21–35%), and 10.0% (36%+). The rate is *higher* in high-immigrant counties. By income bin: **18.7%** (\$0–40K), 11.0%, 12.2%, 4.0% (\$71–90K), and 5.2% (\$91K+). The rate *falls* as income rises. That is the reverse of the abstract (p. 1) and of the Discussion's summary that "it is mostly affluent areas with low immigrant density that have access to TWDL" (p. 21).
- **Specific text claims do not match the table.** [Checkable]
  - p. 11: "counties with median incomes of \$70,000 or greater represented the majority of [TWDL] hot spot locations." Table 2 shows 5 + 8 = 13 of 73 TWDL hot spots (about 18%) in the \$71K+ bins.
  - p. 9: the 36%+ immigrant counties "had the fewest TWDL hot spots." Table 2 shows 7 hot spots in 36%+, against 3 in 0–5%, and a higher rate (10.0% vs. 7.0%).
  - p. 13: TWDL cold spots are "widespread" across Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, and Austin. Table 2 shows only 40 TWDL cold spots statewide (5.6% of 720), and 84% of TWDL campuses are not significant.
  - Figure 5 (p. 13): visually, the TWDL hot spots sit in El Paso, which is shaded in a lower-income class, plus a few scattered points. I could not find any in the dark-green high-income counties.
- **The El Paso concentration is internally inconsistent with Table 2's bins.** [Checkable] The Table 2 note and the Discussion (p. 22) say 69 of 74 TWDL hot spots (93%) are in El Paso County. The bins are county-level (Table 2 note), so all of one county's campuses must fall in a single immigrant-density bin and a single income bin. Yet no immigrant bin holds more than 40 TWDL hot spots, and no income bin holds more than 25. The immigrant-bin hot spots total 74, but the income-bin hot spots total 73; the TWDL campus totals are 720 vs. 716; and the OWDL totals are 1,091 vs. 1,089. Readers cannot tell which figures are right. The inconsistency also means the table cannot be used to judge how much of the county pattern is really El Paso.
- **What "hot spot" measures is not what the abstract claims.** [Interpretive] The Gi* runs only on campuses that already offer the program, with the enrollment ratio as the value (pp. 6–8). A hot spot therefore means neighboring program campuses with high program share of enrollment, roughly whole-school versus strand programs. It does not measure where programs are *placed*, and it does not measure *who* enrolls. The abstract's verb ("TWDL programs cluster in…") reads as placement.
- **Clustering tests do not separate program geography from where ML students live.** [Interpretive] The ANNA benchmark is all public campuses (p. 9). Dual language programs are expected to be more concentrated than schools overall simply because ML students are. "Program-specific spatial forces" (p. 9) is therefore not distinguished from the geography of need. No test uses ML enrollment or all campuses per bin as a denominator, so no per-student or per-campus availability rate can be computed.
- **Some statements cannot be checked.** [Checkable that it is unverifiable] "76% [of TWDL cold spots] located in counties with higher median household income and lower immigrant density" (p. 22) is given as a count over 25 counties. The campus-level Table 2 does not reproduce it. TWDL cold spots in bins of \$56K and above make up 24 of 40 (60%), and in bins of 20% foreign-born or less 23 of 40 (58%).
- **Scope and sample.**
  - [Checkable] Table 1 lists 1,226 TWDL campuses (p. 5), but the analysis uses 729 public TWDL campuses and 1,097 of 1,351 OWDL campuses after excluding charter and alternative campuses (p. 7). The loss of about 40% of TWDL campuses is not broken down.
  - [Checkable] Table 1 gives the identical figure, 1,226, for Early Exit and for TWDL (p. 5), which may be a transcription error.
  - [Interpretive] The data are a single pandemic-era year (2020–21), and the paper does not discuss how that year might affect enrollment ratios.

**Guidance for Readers:**
**Cite this paper for:**

- A first statewide, campus-level map of TWDL and OWDL locations in Texas (2020–21), overlaid on county and tract immigrant density and income (Figures 2–9, pp. 8–17).
- The observation that both program types are overwhelmingly urban and more spatially concentrated than Texas campuses in general (ANN ratios 0.190 and 0.207 vs. 0.317, p. 9). Read this as largely reflecting where ML students live, not as evidence of program-specific sorting.
- The multi-scale finding that in Austin and Houston, TWDL and OWDL hot spots co-locate in moderate-income, immigrant-dense corridors rather than sorting apart (pp. 16–18; Figures 10–13). This is the best-supported and most interesting substantive result.
- A modest descriptive fact in Table 2's "Total" column, which the paper does not stress. TWDL's share of dual language campuses falls as county immigrant density rises: about 45%, 48%, 43%, 37%, and 31% across the five bins (my arithmetic from p. 10). It is highest in the \$91K+ income bin (153 of 307, about 50%, vs. 36–39% elsewhere). That is weak, ecological evidence of relative *program-mix* sorting across counties, and it is the strongest defensible version of the paper's thesis.
- A usable research agenda: availability vs. access at different scales, and dual language vs. early-exit/ESL channeling (p. 23).

**Do not cite it for:**

- "TWDL programs cluster in more affluent, lower-immigrant areas" (abstract). Table 2's hot-spot rates run the other way, and the table note concedes no consistent statewide association outside El Paso.
- Evidence that white or affluent families capture TWDL seats, or that ML students are excluded from TWDL. The study has no student-level or demographic enrollment data. The author says spatial data "cannot follow an individual family through the enrollment process" (p. 23).
- Evidence of gentrification or "extraction" as a process. The design is a single cross-section with no change over time (p. 22 acknowledges the cross-sectional limit).
- Claims that TWDL cold spots show "selective and exclusionary access." Low enrollment ratios can also reflect strand programs on large campuses, which the paper itself allows (p. 13).
- Any statewide quantitative association from Table 2. Its bin totals are internally inconsistent with the El Paso claim.

**Open questions:**

- Does program *presence* (not enrollment intensity) vary with tract demographics once ML enrollment is taken into account? A campus-level model of program offer on tract characteristics and ML counts would answer this directly.
- Who actually enrolls in TWDL strands in Austin, Houston, and El Paso, by ML status, race, and income?
- How did placement change over time relative to neighborhood change? The author proposes exactly this (p. 22).
- Are ML students in dual-language-rich neighborhoods still channeled into early-exit and ESL programs?

**Detailed Commentary:**

**What is new.** The paper's novelty is in its data and scope rather than its methods. The literature on the "gentrification of dual language" that it builds on (Valdés, 1997; Valdez et al., 2016; Chávez-Moreno, 2021; Dorner et al., 2021; Heiman & Murakami, 2019; pp. 3, 21) is mostly qualitative and school- or district-specific. The one distributional precedent cited is Morales and Rao on Illinois (p. 3). A statewide Texas map of both program types at campus level is new, and given that Texas is the largest bilingual-education state after California (p. 4), it is worth having. The spatial tools (ArcGIS average nearest neighbor and Getis-Ord Gi*, pp. 5–8) are standard, so the methodological contribution is small. The paper's statement that it used an LLM for data preparation code (p. 6) is a transparency note, not a methodological contribution.

**Significance at the evidence's real strength.** The question matters. If the integrated, high-status program model reaches ML communities less than the ML-only model does, that is a real equity concern, and the paper's pairing of TWDL with OWDL is the right comparison. But the findings, read at the strength the table supports, are much more modest than the abstract, Discussion (pp. 21–22), and Conclusion (p. 24: "TWDL will continue to follow the geography of white, affluent growth") suggest.

**The quotable claim versus the supported one.** This gap is the central contribution problem, and it is visible on a single page. Table 2 (p. 10) tabulates hot, cold, and not-significant campuses by county bin. For TWDL, the hot-spot rate is highest in the 21–35% foreign-born bin (16.1%) and in the lowest income bin (18.7%), and lowest in the two highest income bins (4.0% and 5.2%). The table note then says 69 of 74 TWDL hot spots are in El Paso County and that excluding El Paso "fewer than 2% of TWDL campuses in any bin are hot spots, indicating no consistent statewide association." The Discussion repeats this (p. 22). El Paso is described in the text as a border county with high immigrant density and low wealth (p. 9). So the one place where TWDL shows intense enrollment is a high-immigrant, lower-income county, which is the opposite of the abstract. The paper nonetheless keeps the abstract, the p. 11 claim that \$70K+ counties hold "the majority" of TWDL hot spots, and the Conclusion's framing. A reader who stops at the abstract, as most citers will, comes away with a claim that the paper's own statistics do not support and partly contradict. [Interpretive] My reading is that the text was written around an earlier analysis and only partly revised after the normalized-ratio Gi* and the El Paso breakdown were added. I cannot confirm this, and it does not change the verdict.

**Figure 9 and the "non-overlapping territories" claim.** Figure 9 (p. 17), which I viewed at high resolution, shows TWDL hot-spot squares mainly at El Paso, with isolated points near the coast and the lower Rio Grande. OWDL hot-spot circles appear in the Dallas-Fort Worth ring and the lower Rio Grande Valley. Grey not-significant symbols dominate the San Antonio–Austin and Houston metros. So the county-level "sorting" in hot-spot terms is essentially an El Paso (TWDL) versus Dallas-Fort Worth and Rio Grande Valley (OWDL) contrast. The paper describes this as "a small cluster near San Antonio" of TWDL hot spots (p. 13), which I could not make out on the figure. That is thin support for a statewide spatial-sorting mechanism. Heavy overplotting of grey symbols in the metros also makes it hard for readers to reconcile the map with Table 2's report that 93% of OWDL campuses are significant hot or cold spots. [Partly interpretive; based on the rendered figure.]

**The defensible version of the thesis lives in a column the paper does not use.** The Total column of Table 2 gives counts of TWDL and OWDL campuses by bin. These show that the mix of dual language programs shifts toward OWDL as county immigrant density rises (TWDL is roughly 45% of dual language campuses in 0–5% counties and 31% in 36%+ counties). They also show TWDL at about half of dual language campuses in the richest bin, against 36–39% in the others. That is a placement pattern, not an enrollment-intensity pattern, and it is modest and not monotone in income. It is county-level, so it is ecological. It is also affected by the bin-total inconsistencies noted above. Still, it is the paper's closest real support for "TWDL tilts toward lower-immigrant, higher-income counties relative to OWDL," and citers who want that claim should cite this, with those caveats, rather than the hot-spot analysis. The Austin map (Figure 10, p. 18) shows something similar at tract level: many not-significant TWDL campuses in the northern suburbs where OWDL campuses are sparse. The paper describes this but does not test it (pp. 17–18).

**Generalizability.** The findings are bounded to Texas, one school year (2020–21), public non-charter campuses, and Texas's specific definitions, under which OWDL serves ML students only (pp. 1, 4). The paper is honest about the tract-level scope limit ("the tract-level findings should be interpreted with that scope boundary in mind," p. 23). It is less careful about the county-level claims, which it generalizes to "the statewide pattern of program type sorting" (p. 15) even though the table note contradicts it. It does not discuss the pandemic year or the exclusion of roughly 40% of the TWDL campuses listed in Table 1 (p. 5 vs. p. 7). I would not carry the county-level pattern to other states, and I would treat the within-metro co-location result as a hypothesis to test elsewhere.

**Standing in the literature.** For the descriptive question "where are Texas's TWDL and OWDL campuses?", this is now the most comprehensive picture I am aware of. For the causal or distributional question it claims to answer ("whose linguistic capital is being centered versus extracted," p. 4), it does not advance beyond the qualitative literature it cites. It does not measure who enrolls, and its spatial statistics do not isolate placement decisions from ML geography. The work that would make this line of evidence decisive has three parts: (a) a campus-level model of program offer on tract demographics and ML counts; (b) enrollment in each program broken down by student demographics, which the author calls for (p. 23); and (c) the longitudinal placement analysis the author proposes (p. 22). Quantitative work on outcomes shows why placement matters: Umansky and Reardon (2014, *AERJ*) on reclassification by program type, and Steele et al. (2017, *AERJ*) on Portland's dual language immersion lotteries. I am confident both exist; neither addresses placement. The ICPSR deposit is noted (p. 24), but the restricted TEA campus data are not included and I could not access the deposit, so I cannot say whether it would resolve the Table 2 inconsistencies.

**Bottom line.** The data assembly and the tract-level co-location finding are real contributions worth citing. But the paper's central, most quotable claim is oversold and partly contradicted by its own tabulation and table note, and the key table cannot be fully reconciled. Under this rubric that is a Weak contribution: a descriptively useful paper whose headline should not travel.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper is better than typical for descriptive GIS work in education. It names its public data sources, reports the key Getis-Ord Gi* parameters (a 170,613 m fixed band, row standardization, an enrollment-ratio input, and the local bands for each city), and deposits a Python data-preparation script and derived shapefiles at ICPSR, with access instructions for the restricted TEA file. But the one quantitative exhibit that could anchor the hot-spot findings, Table 2, cannot be reconciled with several of the paper's own headline statements. The most important is that Table 2's county-level bins rule out the claim that 69 of 74 TWDL hot spots are in El Paso County. The reported sample sizes also do not match the samples the ANNA statistics were actually computed on. So the verifiable part of the claim structure partly contradicts the narrative, and the rest (the map readings, the city-level analyses, and the interactive ArcGIS steps) rests on trust.

**Strengths:**

- **A data deposit exists and is described specifically** (p. 24, Open Practices). It sits in a named repository (AERA Data Repository at ICPSR, DOI 10.3886/ICPSR308283.V1) and contains public data files, derived shapefiles with merged ACS variables, and the Python data-preparation script. The one component that could not be deposited (campus-level TEA program enrollment from a public information request) is named, the reason is given (redistribution restrictions), and a Data Access File with instructions to obtain it is said to be included. By journal-era norms, a deposit plus a documented access pathway earns real credit, and much more than "available upon request."
- **Public inputs are named down to the table.** The paper names ACS B05012 (nativity) and S1903 (median household income), the 2021 ACS vintage, 2021 TIGER/Line county and tract shapefiles, the TEA English Learner Program Report 2020–21, and TEA's campus GIS file (pp. 5–6). It states the immigrant-density formula (foreign-born divided by total population, p. 6) and gives exact choropleth class breaks (p. 6).
- **Most Gi* parameters are stated** (pp. 7–8). These are the input field (program enrollment divided by total campus enrollment), the conceptualization (a fixed distance band of 170,613 m), row standardization, the confidence levels (90/95/99%), the projection (Texas Centric Mapping System–Albers, with Euclidean distance), and the six city-specific bands (Austin 10,824/7,971 m; Houston 7,360/16,448 m; El Paso 5,137/4,956 m). The ANNA study area is stated (695,662 km², p. 7). The Gi* formula is printed correctly (p. 6, checked on the rendered page). The ArcGIS Pro version (3.1) appears in the reference list, under Esri (2022), though not in Methods.
- **ANNA results are reported with the ingredients needed to check them**: the ratio, z, observed and expected mean distances, n, and area (pp. 7, 9). This is what let me detect the sample-size discrepancy described below, which is to the paper's credit.
- **AI use in data preparation is disclosed transparently** (p. 6; Acknowledgements, p. 24), along with the division of labor: the Python prep code was AI-assisted and author-verified, and the spatial statistics were run by the author without AI.

**Weaknesses:**

- **Table 2 is internally inconsistent with the El Paso claim** (checkable; Table 2 note, p. 10; Discussion, p. 22). The note says Table 2's bins are county-level ACS values, and that 69 of 74 TWDL hot spots (93%) are in El Paso County. A single county falls into exactly one immigrant-density bin and one income bin, so one bin in each panel would need at least 69 TWDL hot spots. The largest TWDL hot-spot count in any bin is 40 (21%–35% foreign-born) and 25 (\$0–\$40K). The note's follow-up claim is also contradicted: it says fewer than 2% of TWDL campuses in any bin are hot spots once El Paso is excluded. Whichever bin holds El Paso, the other bins keep their full counts: 3/43 (7.0%) in 0%–5%, 7/104 (6.7%) in 6%–10%, and 17/255 (6.7%) in 11%–20%. So either the bins are not county-level as stated, or the counts or the El Paso claim are wrong. A reader cannot tell which.
- **Several text claims are contradicted by Table 2, the paper's only tabulation of the hot-spot results** (checkable):
  - p. 9: counties at 36%+ foreign-born "had the fewest TWDL hot spots." Table 2 shows 7 hot spots (10.0%) in 36%+ against 3 (7.0%) in 0%–5%. By rate, 36%+ is the second-highest bin.
  - p. 11: TWDL counties with median income of \$70,000 or more "represented the majority of hot spot locations." Table 2 shows 5 + 8 = 13 of 73 hot spots (18%).
  - p. 11: the \$91,000+ counties "show almost no OWDL hot spots." Table 2 shows 73 of 154 (47.4%).
  - p. 10: the lowest-immigrant-density counties "show almost no OWDL hot spots." Table 2 shows 25 of 53 (47.2%) in 0%–5%.
  - Some of these sentences refer to hot spots "at 99% confidence," and Table 2 collapses the 90/95/99% levels (note, p. 10). Those claims are therefore uncheckable rather than strictly contradicted, but the table as published does not support them.
- **Reported sample sizes do not match the analyzed samples** (checkable). The text gives n = 729 TWDL and 1,097 OWDL for the ANNA (p. 7). The reported expected distances (15,542 m and 12,626 m, p. 9) and z-scores imply n = 720 and 1,091 exactly, which is 729 − 9 and 1,097 − 6: the geometry-error exclusions from the Table 2 note (p. 10). So the ANNA was run on the post-exclusion samples, while the paper reports the pre-exclusion ns.
- **The two Table 2 panels have different totals, with no explanation** (checkable). The immigrant-density panel sums to 720 TWDL and 1,091 OWDL campuses. The income panel sums to 716 and 1,089. The four missing TWDL campuses are 1 hot spot and 3 not-significant; the two missing OWDL campuses are both hot spots. A possible cause (my inference, not verifiable) is that the published income bins have \$1,000 gaps (\$40,001–\$40,999, \$55,001–\$55,999, and so on, p. 6), which would leave counties with medians inside a gap unbinned.
- **The path from Table 1 to the analytic sample is not documented.** TWDL goes from 1,226 campuses (Table 1, p. 5) to 729 (p. 7), a loss of 497 (40.5%). OWDL goes from 1,351 to 1,097, a loss of 254 (18.8%). The only stated reason is "Charter and alternative campuses were excluded" (p. 7). Rebuilding the sample needs a charter/alternative flag, its source and year (for example, TEA campus type or charter status codes), and the order of steps (joins, missing coordinates, missing enrollment, suppression). The paper gives none of these and no count at any step. Whether charters and alternative campuses alone could account for two-fifths of TWDL campuses cannot be judged from the paper. The asymmetry between the program types (40% vs. 19%) itself needs explaining.
- **Table 1 and the accompanying text do not agree** (checkable). The text says the report shows "8,115 bilingual programs" across 7,134 schools (p. 5). Table 1's rows sum to 13,865 (all six types) or 4,267 (the four bilingual types). Neither equals 8,115. TWDL (1,226) is identical to Early Exit Transitional Bilingual (1,226) in Table 1, which may be a transcription error. That matters because 1,226 is the denominator for the TWDL sample loss.
- **The ANNA reference population is ambiguous.** The all-campus reference is labeled "all public campuses (n = 7,134)" (pp. 7, 9). On p. 5, 7,134 is the count of schools in the English Learner Program Report, not all Texas public campuses. The paper does not say whether it includes charters, which were excluded from the TWDL and OWDL samples. The reported ratio and z (0.317, −109.94) imply n ≈ 7,069–7,090 under Esri's formula, allowing for rounding of the ratio, which is also short of 7,134. This comparison underpins the claim that clustering "exceeds what general school geography alone would predict" (p. 9).
- **The Gi* specification is incomplete in places that change classifications**:
  - Whether ArcGIS's FDR correction was applied is not stated.
  - The Incremental Spatial Autocorrelation settings (start distance, increment, number of bands) are not given, and neither is which dataset's peak produced the single 170,613 m band "applied to the TWDL and OWDL datasets" (p. 8).
  - How the local bands were obtained ("allowing ArcGIS Pro to calculate") and how each city subset was delimited (city limits, ISD, county, or metro) are not stated, and no per-city n is given.
  - The source and year of the "total campus enrollment" denominator are not given.
  - How suppressed values were handled is mentioned as a data-preparation step (p. 6) but not described.
  - The input variable is described inconsistently: "number of students enrolled" on p. 6 versus a normalized ratio on p. 8.
  - "Hot spot analyses were conducted at both the county and census tract levels" (p. 8) reads as if polygons were analyzed. Table 2's campus counts indicate the Gi* was run on campus points, with counties and tracts only as overlays.
- **The spatial statistics were run interactively and are not scripted.** The deposit is described as containing the data-preparation script only (p. 24), and the ArcGIS Pro analyses were run by hand (p. 6). The paper does not say whether an ArcPy script, ModelBuilder model, or geoprocessing history exported with the tool parameters was deposited. Even with the restricted TEA file in hand, the ANNA and Gi* steps would have to be rebuilt from the prose above.
- **The ACS citations contradict the text.** The text specifies 2021 ACS 5-year estimates (p. 6), but the reference URLs point to 1-year tables (`ACSDT1Y2021.B05012` and `ACSST1Y2021.S1903`, reference list, p. 26). 1-year estimates are not published for tracts, so the text is presumably right, but a replicator following the citations would pull the wrong product. S1903 is also a Subject Table, not a "Detailed Table" as the text says. The TIGER/Line citation (a 2020 technical document) does not match the 2021 shapefiles used. The TEA campus GIS file is not cited or dated. The in-text citation "Hot Spot Analysis," 2023 (p. 8) has no entry in the reference list.
- **Most findings are map readings with no tabulated support.** The county narratives (pp. 9–15) and the city-level Austin, Houston, and El Paso results (pp. 15–21, Figures 10–15) are reported only as maps. There are no counts of hot, cold, and not-significant campuses by city, no z-score summaries, and no sample sizes. The "25 counties" and "76%" cold-spot claim (p. 22) cannot be checked against anything in the paper. For TWDL cold spots, the Table 2 campus shares at \$56K+ and \$71K+ are 60% and 38%.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Treat the Table 2 findings as unverified until the inconsistencies are resolved.** Before relying on the claim that TWDL hot spots are concentrated in affluent, low-immigrant counties, or on the statement that 93% of them are in El Paso, a reader should obtain the campus-level Gi* output and confirm three things:
  - which bin El Paso campuses fall into,
  - whether the bins are county- or tract-level,
  - why the income panel has 4 fewer TWDL and 2 fewer OWDL campuses.
- **Note that Table 2 leans the other way from the abstract.** The rates are highest in the \$0–\$40K bin (18.7%) and the 21%–35% foreign-born bin (16.1%) (p. 10). The table note itself concludes there is "no consistent statewide association" outside El Paso. Readers should weigh the abstract's claim that TWDL "cluster[s] in more affluent, lower-immigrant areas" (p. 1) against the table rather than the prose.
- **To get the missing specification details, ask the author or check the deposit's documentation for:**
  1. a sample-flow table from the TEA public information request file through the TEA GIS join, charter/alternative exclusion, missing coordinates or enrollment, suppression, and geometry errors, down to 720 and 1,091;
  2. the charter and alternative flag and its source;
  3. the total-enrollment denominator source and the suppression rule;
  4. the Incremental Spatial Autocorrelation settings, the FDR setting, and the ArcGIS geoprocessing history for each Gi* and ANNA run;
  5. the city-subset boundaries and n;
  6. the composition of the 7,134-campus ANNA reference.
- **Rebuild the ACS layer independently. It is fully public.** Pull the 2017–2021 ACS 5-year B05012 and S1903 for Texas counties and tracts. Check the stated unweighted means (9.3% and 16.7% immigrant density; \$57,221 and \$71,408 median income; p. 7) and assign El Paso County to its bins. That alone can settle which part of the Table 2 note is wrong.
- **Do not treat the ANNA comparison as more than descriptive.** The TWDL and OWDL statistics check out arithmetically for n = 720 and 1,091. The all-campus baseline's n is unclear, and ANN ratios for point sets of very different sizes within a fixed state-wide study area are not directly comparable measures of "program-specific" clustering. The inferential step on p. 9 cannot be checked from what is reported.
- **Treat the city-level findings (Austin, Houston, El Paso) as effectively unverifiable as reported.** They rest only on maps, with no counts, no subset definitions, and no n.

**Detailed Commentary:**

#### Data availability
The data architecture is a common and legitimate education-research case: public geography and census inputs, plus one restricted administrative file (campus-level program enrollment obtained by public information request; pp. 5, 24). The author handled this appropriately at the policy level. The derived and public files are deposited, the restricted file is identified, and an access pathway is documented (p. 24). I did not access the deposit and do not assess its contents. What the paper does not make clear is whether the public information request is re-requestable in identical form, meaning the same fields, year, and suppression, or whether a replicator would receive a differently masked file. That determines whether the enrollment-ratio input can be rebuilt exactly.

#### Code and software environment
Data preparation (ID cleaning, enrollment ratios, suppression handling, ACS–TIGER merges) was done in Python with AI assistance and is deposited (pp. 6, 24). This is the best-documented stage. The substantive statistics, the ANNA and Gi* runs, were done interactively in ArcGIS Pro (p. 6), version 3.1 per the reference list (Esri, 2022; p. 25). Several defaults matter for Gi*, including the FDR correction, the self-neighbor handling that is inherent to Gi*, and the Incremental Spatial Autocorrelation search settings, and they are not stated. The paper does not say that a script or tool log for these steps was deposited. This is the main gap between "the data can be rebuilt" and "the results can be regenerated."

#### Sample construction (check a)
The chain is: Table 1 (p. 5), 1,226 TWDL and 1,351 OWDL campuses; text (p. 7), 729 and 1,097 "public" campuses after excluding charter and alternative campuses; Table 2 note (p. 10), minus 9 and 6 for geometry errors, giving 720 and 1,091, which the immigrant-density panel sums to exactly. The last step is documented and reconciles. The first step is not. It removes 497 TWDL campuses (40.5%) and 254 OWDL campuses (18.8%) on a one-sentence rule with no flag definition, no source, and no intermediate counts. Charters and alternative campuses are a modest share of Texas campuses overall. Whether they could make up two-fifths of TWDL campuses is a question the paper does not answer and that I cannot answer from the text (interpretive). Two further facts complicate the starting point. Table 1's TWDL count duplicates the Early Exit count exactly, and the "8,115 programs" in the text matches no sum of Table 1. Both suggest the starting counts themselves need checking. The word "public" is also ambiguous, since Texas charters are public schools.

#### Gi* specification (check b)
Stated: the input field (the ratio; p. 8), the fixed distance band of 170,613 m chosen by ISA (p. 8), row standardization (p. 8), the 90/95/99% bins (p. 8), the projection (p. 7), the local bands (p. 8), and the formula (p. 6). Missing or ambiguous:

- the FDR correction (on or off);
- the ISA inputs and which dataset's peak was used;
- the denominator source;
- the suppression treatment (only mentioned, p. 6);
- the city-subset definitions and n;
- how the local bands were derived;
- the version in Methods, where only the reference list gives it.

The p. 6 description of the input field ("number of students enrolled") contradicts p. 8 (a ratio). Separately, and as a checkable fact, the resulting classifications are very different by program type. Only 81 of 1,091 OWDL campuses (7.4%) are not significant, against 606 of 720 TWDL campuses (84.2%) (Table 2, immigrant panel). With a 170 km band and row standardization, each campus's local sum covers a large region. A replicator should expect FDR and band choice to move many classifications, which makes the unstated FDR setting consequential (interpretive).

#### ANNA arithmetic (check c)
Esri's expected distance is D_E = 0.5 / sqrt(n/A) and its standard error is 0.26136 / sqrt(n²/A). The checks are listed below. The TWDL and OWDL ANNA statistics are internally consistent, but only for n = 720 and 1,091, not the stated 729 and 1,097.

#### Table 2 sums (check d)
Every row sums correctly: hot + cold + not significant equals the total in all 20 rows. Across bins, the immigrant panel gives 74/40/606 (TWDL) and 587/423/81 (OWDL). The income panel gives 73/40/603 and 585/423/81. The cold-spot totals agree across panels. The hot-spot and not-significant totals do not, and neither panel's total matches the other. The 74 TWDL hot spots in the immigrant panel match the note's "69 of 74." Under the stated county-level binning, though, El Paso's 69 cannot fit in any single bin, as shown above.

#### ACS and TEA sources (check e)
The text specifies 2021 ACS 5-year estimates, and the stated reason (tract and small-county reliability) is correct (p. 6). The references cite 1-year table IDs (p. 26), which cannot supply tract data, so the references are wrong rather than the analysis. The paper does not say whether the 5-year S1903 subject table or the detailed table B19013 was used for median income. That matters little for values but matters for exact replication. The TEA sources are:

- the English Learner Program Report 2020–21, cited with a URL (TEA, 2021b);
- the campus-level public information request data, uncited but described;
- the TEA GIS campus locations, uncited and undated, described only as TEA's "open public data site" (p. 6).

The TIGER/Line vintage in the text (2021) and the reference (2020 technical documentation) differ. This is harmless for the counties, since 2021 ACS uses 2020 tract geography, but it should be reconciled.

#### Checkable facts I verified

1. **ANNA expected distance, TWDL (p. 9).** At the stated n = 729 and A = 695,662 km², D_E = 15,446 m, against a reported 15,542 m. Solving for n from 15,542 m gives n = 720.0 (729 − 9). Mismatch with the stated n; exact match with the post-exclusion n.
2. **ANNA expected distance, OWDL (p. 9).** At the stated n = 1,097, D_E = 12,591 m, against a reported 12,626 m. The implied n = 1,091.0 (1,097 − 6). Same pattern.
3. **ANNA z-scores (p. 9).** Using Esri's standard error, TWDL gives z = −42.12 at n = 729 and −41.60 at n = 720; the reported value is −41.60. OWDL gives −50.36 at n = 1,097 and −50.08 at n = 1,091; the reported value is −50.08. This confirms the ANNA used the post-exclusion samples.
4. **ANN ratios (p. 9).** 2,946/15,542 = 0.1896 (reported 0.190) and 2,619/12,626 = 0.2074 (reported 0.207). Consistent. "Approximately 40% lower than the baseline": 0.190/0.317 = 0.60 (40% lower) and 0.207/0.317 = 0.65 (35% lower). Roughly consistent.
5. **All-campus ANNA (p. 9).** For a ratio of 0.317 (rounding range 0.3165–0.3175) and z = −109.94, the implied n is 7,069–7,090, not the stated 7,134. D_E is not reported, so this is weaker evidence (inference), but it suggests the reference sample also differs from its stated n.
6. **Table 2 row sums (p. 10).** All 20 rows reconcile.
7. **Table 2 panel totals (p. 10).** The immigrant panel sums to TWDL 720 and OWDL 1,091, matching 729 − 9 and 1,097 − 6. The income panel sums to TWDL 716 and OWDL 1,089, a shortfall of 4 and 2 with no explanation. Hot spots: TWDL 74 against 73, OWDL 587 against 585. Not significant: TWDL 606 against 603, OWDL 81 against 81. Cold spots: 40 and 423 in both panels.
8. **El Paso claim against Table 2 (p. 10 note; p. 22).** 69 of 74 TWDL hot spots would require one bin in each panel to hold at least 69. The maximums are 40 (immigrant) and 25 (income). The "<2% outside El Paso" claim is contradicted by at least two of the three bins 0%–5% (7.0%), 6%–10% (6.7%), and 11%–20% (6.7%), whichever bin El Paso occupies.
9. **Text against Table 2.** On p. 9, the "fewest TWDL hot spots" are said to be at 36%+, but Table 2 shows 7 there against 3 at 0%–5%. On p. 11, TWDL hot spots at \$70K+ are called a "majority," but they are 13/73 = 18%. On p. 11, OWDL hot spots at \$91K+ are "almost no," but they are 73/154 = 47.4%. On p. 10, OWDL hot spots at the lowest density are "almost no," but they are 25/53 = 47.2% (the text partly qualifies this to 99% confidence, which Table 2 does not separate).
10. **TWDL cold spots against the p. 22 "76%" claim.** From Table 2 (income panel), 24/40 = 60% of TWDL cold-spot campuses are in \$56K+ counties and 15/40 = 37.5% in \$71K+ counties. The 76% figure may be a share of counties (25 counties), which is not tabulated anywhere and so cannot be checked.
11. **Table 1 against the text (p. 5).** Table 1 sums to 13,865 (all types) or 4,267 (bilingual types only), and neither equals the stated 8,115 programs. TWDL = Early Exit = 1,226 exactly.
12. **Sample loss from Table 1 to the analysis sample (pp. 5, 7).** TWDL loses 497 of 1,226 (40.5%) and OWDL 254 of 1,351 (18.8%). The only documented reason is the charter/alternative exclusion.
13. **Gi* formula (p. 6, rendered).** It is printed in the standard Esri form, with the numerator Σw_ij·x_j − X̄·Σw_ij and the denominator S·sqrt([nΣw_ij² − (Σw_ij)²]/(n−1)). It is correct. X̄ and S are not defined in the text but are standard.
14. **Citations.** The ACS references use 1-year table IDs (`ACSDT1Y2021`, `ACSST1Y2021`) although the text uses 5-year estimates. "Hot Spot Analysis," 2023 (p. 8) is missing from the reference list. ArcGIS Pro 3.1 is cited only in the reference list (Esri, 2022).
